intro: Twelve verses with a hinge you can hear. The first half is a man lying down among lions; the second half is the same man with a harp, and the two are joined by the refrain of verse 6, which returns unchanged as verse 12. Verses 8 to 12 turn up again, almost word for word, as the opening of Psalm 108, so this ending had a life of its own outside this psalm. The superscription puts it in a cave while David runs from Saul, and the book of Samuel gives him two caves, Adullam in chapter 22 and En Gedi in chapter 24, without saying which one this is.

stichs.en: For the leader; al tashchet.
Of David, a michtam,
when he fled from Saul, in the cave.

verses.summary: Four labels stacked before the psalm starts: a tune, an author, a genre word and a scene. Two of the four are not understood, and the scene is the only one that dates it.

stichs.en: Be gracious to me, God, be gracious to me,
for in You my soul has taken refuge;
and in the shadow of Your wings I will take refuge,
until the destruction passes by.

verses.summary: The plea is doubled, then given a reason. What is asked for is the smallest cover in the book, a bird's wing, and it is asked for only until something has finished passing overhead.

stichs.en: I call to God Most High,
to the God who carries it through for me.

verses.summary: Two names for God across one line, and a participle that means finishing rather than beginning. What is requested is completion of something already under way.

stichs.en: He will send from heaven and save me,
he who pants after me has taunted. Selah.
God will send His kindness and His truth.

glosses: the one who pants after me
verses.summary: The verb of sending frames the verse, and what is sent the second time is not an army. Kindness and truth arrive as the specific answer to an insult.

stichs.en: My soul is among lions,
let me lie down among those who blaze,
sons of man whose teeth are a spear and arrows,
and their tongue a sharp sword.

verses.summary: The image is not left as an image. It is decoded inside the verse: the lions are people, and the parts that maim are the mouth twice over, teeth and then tongue.

stichs.en: Be exalted above the heavens, God;
over all the earth, Your glory.

verses.summary: The refrain cuts into a complaint that has not been settled. Nothing in the cave has changed; the request is only that God be high enough to be seen from it.

stichs.en: They set a net for my steps,
my soul was bowed down;
they dug a pit before me,
they fell into the middle of it. Selah.

verses.summary: Two hunting devices and one reversal. The pit takes the diggers, and that is the only rescue the psalm ever reports as having happened.

stichs.en: My heart is steady, God,
my heart is steady;
let me sing and make music.

verses.summary: The turn, and it is built out of the same doubling verse 2 used for the plea. The identical device now carries steadiness where it once carried need.

stichs.en: Awake, my glory;
awake, harp and lyre;
let me wake the dawn.

verses.summary: Three wakings in one verse: himself, the instruments, then the dawn. The last one changes person, from an imperative to a first person verb, so the sun is not asked but woken.

stichs.en: I will thank You among the peoples, my Lord;
I will sing to You among the nations.

verses.summary: The room widens from a cave to the nations in a single verse. A man in hiding from one king undertakes to sing where everyone can hear him.

stichs.en: For Your kindness is great, up to the heavens,
and Your truth up to the skies.

verses.summary: The two things sent in verse 4 are measured here, and the measurement is vertical. They already reach the height the refrain asks God to rise to.

stichs.en: Be exalted above heavens, God;
over all the earth, Your glory.

verses.summary: The refrain returns with one difference: the definite article on the word for heavens is gone. The same sentence, said now by a man who has already started singing.

pardes.body: Two halves and a repeated line. Verses 2 to 5 are pursuit: refuge asked for, an insult received, teeth and tongues described. Verses 8 to 11 are music: a steady heart, instruments woken, an audience of nations. Between them sits verse 6, and the same words close the psalm as verse 12. Verse 7 is the pivot in the plot rather than in the mood, because it is the one place where something actually happens: the trap works on the trappers. Notice that nothing in the man's situation is reported as changed between verse 5 and verse 8. He is still in the cave. What changes is the heart, and the psalm gives that its own word, {{8.0}}, meaning set firm or established.

Three words in the first line are unsettled. {{1.2}} belongs to the phrase al tashchet, do not destroy, which stands over Psalms 57, 58, 59 and 75 and is generally taken as the name of a known tune rather than as a prayer. {{1.4}}, michtam, heads six psalms and has been derived from a root for gold, for inscription and for covering, with no agreement. Inside the psalm, {{2.5}} is a feminine perfect with an unusual ending, and {{5.4}}, those who blaze, is hard enough that translators split between people who are on fire, people who devour, and a word for flames. The clearest crux is {{7.3}}: the verb has no expressed subject, so the line reads either as the enemies bowing my soul down or as my soul being bowed, and both readings are in print. Verses 8 to 12 recur as Psalm 108:2 to 6, which is a fact about the manuscripts rather than a theory.

The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, tells of a harp that hung above David's bed and sounded on its own when the north wind struck it at midnight, so that he rose and studied until morning. Verse 9 is read there against the plain sense of a man waking up: he wakes the dawn, the dawn does not wake him. That reading takes {{9.5}} at full strength, as a transitive verb with {{9.6}} as its object, which is what the Hebrew actually has. The cave in the superscription is read as the setting for the whole psalm, so that the promise to sing among the nations in verse 10 is made by a man with no audience at all, and the refrain asking God to rise above the heavens is said by someone underground. Where the psalm is applied to Israel rather than to David, the lions of verse 5 become the empires, and the pit of verse 7 becomes the standard image for a plan that turns on its planner.

The shadow of the wings in verse 2 is read as protection that works by proximity rather than by strength: a shadow requires no wall, only nearness to something that stands between you and the light. In this reading the word rendered my glory in verse 9 is the soul rather than reputation, so the three wakings of that verse are a sequence: the soul wakes first, then the instruments of the body, then the world outside. Waking the dawn is then the claim that the inner order precedes the outer one, and that the day begins where a person begins it. The two halves of the psalm are the same person at two depths, which is why the refrain can be said unchanged from either.
